strengths: Makes an important conceptual contribution distinguishing unfaithfulness from incompleteness in CoT evaluation
Comprehensive multi-method empirical evaluation using Filler Tokens, FUR, faithful@k, Logit Lens, and causal mediation analysis
Novel faithful@k metric cleverly adapts sampling-based evaluation to address greedy decoding assumptions
Thorough experimental documentation across 3 models, 3 datasets, and 3 hint types with detailed hyperparameter reporting
Well-motivated critique of Biasing Features metric that conflates orthogonal concepts
Honest discussion of computational limitations and methodological limitations (LLM-judge reliability, sample sizes)
weaknesses: Limited to small models (3-8B parameters) with no evaluation on larger reasoning models despite those being the focus of recent unfaithfulness claims
Inconsistent results across alternative metrics raise questions about why they disagree so substantially (Filler Tokens 20-40%, FUR 50%+, but varies widely)
Puzzling divergence in faithful@k results: Professor hint shows strong improvement with k while Metadata/Black Squares plateau, suggesting mechanisms more complex than token budget incompleteness
Small effect sizes in causal mediation analysis (many estimates 1e-6 to 1e-7) with unclear practical significance despite statistical significance
LLM-as-judge achieves only 31% recall/precision for positive cases, missing many actual hint verbalizations and potentially weakening claims
Critical sample size issues in several conditions (Llama-3-8B with Black Squares: n=3-5 instances) undermining statistical reliability
Post-hoc rationalization analysis underdeveloped: direct effects often exceed indirect effects and late-layer hint emergence could support post-hoc claims rather than refute them
Results highly heterogeneous across models (Gemma reaches 0.9 faithful@k under Professor but 0 under Metadata; Llama-3-8B consistently lower) without explanation for why
Dataset scope limited to multiple-choice reasoning tasks; generalization to open-ended generation or other domains unclear
Artificial hint setup (random injected cues) limits insights into whether models actually rely on decision-relevant factors in real use

strengths: Addresses an important and timely debate about CoT faithfulness with comprehensive experimental validation across multiple metrics, models (3B-70B), and datasets

Introduces novel diagnostic metric (faithful@k) that can distinguish incompleteness from unfaithfulness through differential behavior across hint types, and novel application of Causal Mediation Analysis
Comprehensive empirical coverage with multiple complementary faithfulness metrics (Biasing Features, Filler Tokens, FUR) and extensive robustness checks addressing methodological concerns
Clear, measured framing that avoids overclaiming—argues that absence of hint verbalization doesn't prove unfaithfulness rather than claiming all CoTs are faithful
Shows non-trivial fraction (50%+) of Biasing Features-flagged unfaithful CoTs are classified as faithful by alternative metrics across models and datasets
weaknesses: LLM-as-judge achieves only 36% precision and 31% recall, substantially undermining confidence in the ~80% unfaithfulness rates in Figure 2 that motivate the paper, even though false negatives are partially addressed

Causal Mediation Analysis effect sizes are often very small (e-6 to e-11 scale) with unclear practical significance; NIE and NDE sometimes have overlapping confidence intervals, making interpretation difficult

Faithful@k cannot distinguish incompleteness from non-exhaustiveness (acknowledged by authors); the explanation for differential behavior across hint types (sycophancy) is speculative and not definitively validated

Qualitative examples in Table 6 show CoTs with factually incorrect reasoning and problematic semantic reinterpretations (e.g., 'electrical path' → 'open'), which undermine rather than support main thesis; only 4 examples provided
Limited scope to artificial constrained setting (multi-hop QA with 2-4 multiple choice answers); generalization to open-ended reasoning, code generation, or long-form tasks unclear
Somewhat incremental contribution as recent work (Barez et al., Korbak et al.) already advocates for broader evaluation approaches and acknowledges communication utility of CoTs
Lacks human evaluation of CoT quality, analysis of correlation with downstream task performance, and practical guidance for practitioners on how to use findings
